label: The Cotangent Bundle
notes: This chapter, printed pages 272 to 303, turns the tangent space inside out. Where Chapter 3 gave vectors, here we meet covectors: linear measuring devices on tangent vectors. We will build the cotangent space, the differential of a function, pullbacks, and line integrals, ending with the closed-versus-exact question.

label: Covectors and the Dual Space
notes: A covector at a point is just a linear functional on the tangent space, so the cotangent space is the dual vector space. Stress that no metric is needed: a covector eats a vector and returns a number. Picture it as a stack of parallel level hyperplanes that a vector pierces.

label: The Coordinate Coframe
notes: Each chart gives a basis of covectors, the differentials of the coordinate functions. They are dual to the coordinate vector fields: dx-i applied to partial-j is the Kronecker delta. Any covector expands in this coframe, and its components are read off by pairing against the coordinate vectors.

label: Pairing as Counting Crossings
notes: The most useful mental image: a covector is a ruled stack of hyperplanes, and its value on a vector counts how many sheets that vector crosses. This makes linearity obvious and shows why covectors and vectors are different species. Walk through the dual coframe acting on coordinate vectors here.

label: Change of Coordinates
notes: Covector components transform by the Jacobian transpose, contravariantly to vector components. Derive dx-tilde from the chain rule on coordinate functions. Emphasize that the pairing of a covector with a vector is coordinate independent: the two transformation rules are inverse-transpose and cancel exactly.

label: The Cotangent Bundle T*M
notes: Assembling all cotangent spaces gives a smooth rank-n vector bundle, the cotangent bundle. Its local trivializations come from coordinate coframes, and the transition functions are the inverse-transpose duals of the tangent bundle's. A smooth covector field, or one-form, is a smooth section of this bundle.

label: The Differential df
notes: For a smooth real function, the differential df is the one-form whose value on a vector is that vector applied as a derivation: df(X) equals Xf. In coordinates df is the row of partial derivatives. This is the coordinate-free first derivative, living naturally as a covector, not a vector.

label: df as Best Linear Approximation
notes: The differential is the linear part of the change in f. Its kernel is the tangent plane to the level set through the point, and the level hyperplanes of df are level sets of f to first order. The residual of the linear approximation decays quadratically with step size, as the notebook checks.

label: Pullback of Covectors
notes: Unlike vector fields, covector fields always pull back along any smooth map. The pullback dualizes the differential of the map, sending covectors on the target back to covectors on the source. The fundamental identity is that the pullback of dh equals d of h composed with the map. Restriction to submanifolds is a special case.

label: Line Integrals of One-Forms
notes: A line integral of a one-form along a curve is ordinary integration after pulling the form back to the parameter interval. It is reparametrization invariant up to orientation. This is the natural pairing of a one-form against a curve, and it is the bridge to the conservative-versus-exact discussion.

label: Conservative and Exact Forms
notes: A one-form is conservative when its line integral depends only on endpoints, equivalently when every loop integral vanishes. Exact means it is the differential of a function. The fundamental theorem for line integrals shows exact implies conservative, and integrating from a base point recovers a potential for any conservative form.

label: Closed Versus Exact
notes: Closed is the local derivative test: in the plane, P dx plus Q dy is closed when the mixed partials match. Every exact form is closed. The converse fails globally: the angular form on the punctured plane is closed but has loop integral two pi, so topology obstructs exactness. Poincare's lemma rescues us on star-shaped domains.

label: The Angular Form and Winding
notes: The angular one-form is the canonical closed-but-not-exact example. Around a loop winding k times about the origin its integral is two pi k. That single integer is the obstruction: it measures the hole the punctured plane carries. This is the first taste of de Rham cohomology to come.

label: Recap and Connections
notes: Recap the chain: covectors measure vectors, the coframe dx-i is dual to the coordinate vectors, df is the coordinate-free derivative, pullbacks always exist, and line integrals separate exact, conservative, and closed forms. Chapter 10 frames T*M as a bundle; Chapter 13 adds a metric to bridge covectors and vectors.
